items.title: Beyond Static Credentials: Reddit’s Journey to Workload Identity and mTLS
items.summary: Written by Pratik Lotia How we introduced automatically rotated workload credentials and migrated an existing service fleet to mutual TLS without a coordinated cutover. One Service, Several Sets Of Credentials Imagine building a new internal service. It calls another service, requires user context, reads from a database, requires access to a cloud resource and publishes events. Each dependency may have a different answer to the same question: how does the caller prove who it is and how do you manage access control? With static credentials, the answer usually involves provisioning a secret, deciding where to store it, granting access to the consumers of the secret, setting up authorization rules and wiring it into the application. Repeat that for every dependency and for every Kubernetes cluster or cloud environment it deploys to. The service is eventually ready to run, but its credentials still need coordination across multiple teams making it a high friction and time consuming process. When a security control is cumbersome enough, your customers will often find a way to bypass it or adopt less practices which leads to other issues such leaking credentials in code, sharing tokens and lack of regular rotation. We had accumulated versions of this problem across our infrastructure. Service authentication used static tokens. Database integrations had their own credential workflows. Services with an existing TLS requirement maintained separate certificate integrations. Depending on the system, credential onboarding could take weeks. There was also an operational problem where a service that received an unexpected burst of requests, couldn’t reliably identify the caller, let alone deny access to a caller. The goal was a common identity system for workloads, with short-lived credentials issued and rotated automatically. We wanted the same foundation to work for service calls and infrastructure access, rather than asking each integration to introduce another secret. Read on to find out how we succeeded in getting rid of static secrets for our modern database stack and getting 90% of our in-cluster Go grpc traffic to use authenticated calls in the form of mutual TLS. Making The Work Worth Adopting A project that changes how services authenticate needs support well beyond the security team. We had to make the case to leadership and partner teams that the investment would help them with product velocity. For product teams expanding an existing service, moving it to a new environment or launching a new one, use of a common identity system would significantly speed up product launches. Instead of designing another way to issue, distribute, and rotate client credentials, platform teams could build on the shared identity system and focus on deciding who should have access. This work stretched across multiple quarters and became one of the first real, sustained partnerships between Security, Platform and Product at Reddit. We chose mTLS to provide verified identities, confidentiality, and integrity through one shared integration, rather than asking teams to migrate again when they needed encrypted communication. We started with teams that had needs like: a maintained TLS integration for sensitive services, fewer credential-provisioning steps, and a way to identify callers. Some early adopters already used TLS through a bespoke certificate path and wanted to move away from its scaling and maintenance constraints. For them, the value was replacing an existing operational dependency with something shared. Performance was another reasonable concern. Modern TLS is fast but benchmarking your integrations for TLS connection establishment, certificate acquisition, latency and distinguishing those costs from steady-state request processing goes a long way in convincing product teams. Adoption also needed an owner. Publishing a migration guide gave teams instructions, but it did not create room on their roadmaps. We eventually took on preparing migration changes ourselves, with service owners reviewing and validating the behavior they knew best. That decision substantially changed the amount of work we could complete. Choosing SPIFFE And SPIRE We had already invested in moving service communication to gRPC. Our identity model needed to fit into that foundation. We also wanted to avoid vendor lock-in. We chose SPIFFE as the identity standard and SPIRE as its implementation. SPIFFE defines how a workload identity is represented and how software obtains and verifies credentials for it. SPIRE performs the attestation and issuance work. The SPIFFE community’s book, Solving the Bottom Turtle, is a useful introduction to the problem and the design. We considered introducing a service mesh that provides mTLS along with routing, retries, and other traffic controls.
